text: Nine countries hold about 12,187 nuclear warheads, and about 9,745 of them are in military stockpiles ready for use. These are estimates.
source_name: Federation of American Scientists, Status of World Nuclear Forces, 2026

text: The number of warheads in military stockpiles is rising again after decades of falling. The world total peaked at about 70,300 in 1986.
source_name: Federation of American Scientists, Status of World Nuclear Forces, 2026

text: A full-scale US–Russia nuclear war, modelled with about 4,400 weapons, would kill about 360 million people directly. Soot blocking sunlight would then cut global crop calories by about 90% three to four years later, and more than 5 billion people would die of hunger.
source_name: Xia et al., Nature Food, 2022 (Rutgers University summary)

text: Even a smaller India–Pakistan war with about 100 weapons is modelled at about 27 million direct deaths and about 255 million deaths from famine within two years.
source_name: Xia et al., Nature Food, 2022 (via CBS News)

text: Philosopher Toby Ord puts the chance that nuclear war causes an existential catastrophe this century at about 1 in 1,000. He says estimates like this could easily be 3 times higher or lower.
source_name: Toby Ord, The Precipice, 2020 (Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews)

text: In a 2022 forecasting tournament, the median chance of a nuclear catastrophe by 2100 was 4% among superforecasters and 8% among domain experts.
source_name: Forecasting Research Institute, Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament, 2022 (FRI write-up of nuclear results)

text: The same tournament put the chance of human extinction from nuclear weapons by 2100 at 0.074% (superforecasters) and 0.55% (domain experts).
source_name: Forecasting Research Institute, Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament, 2022 (FRI write-up of nuclear results)

text: The world total has fallen about 83% since the 1986 peak, from about 70,300 to about 12,187 warheads (EarthOS calculation from the two published figures).
source_name: Federation of American Scientists, Status of World Nuclear Forces, 2026

text: New START, the last binding limit on US and Russian arsenals, has expired. The US says it wants a new treaty that also covers China and all Russian warheads, not only the deployed strategic ones.
source_name: Brookings Institution, Steven Pifer, What comes after New START?

text: Whether a regional war would cause a global nuclear winter is contested. For about 100 Hiroshima-sized weapons, one research group (Mills et al.) finds a nuclear winter and another at Los Alamos (Reisner et al.) finds none.
source_name: Hess, Nagasaki University RECNA working paper, 2020

text: Superforecasters and domain experts in the 2022 tournament were nearly 10 times apart on the chance of nuclear extinction.
source_name: Forecasting Research Institute, Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament, 2022 (FRI write-up of nuclear results)

text: In the modelled wars most deaths come from hunger, not blast, because soot cuts crop and fishery output worldwide. This topic feeds directly into food security.
source_name: Xia et al., Nature Food, 2022 (Rutgers University summary)

text: The UN lists artificial intelligence among the new technologies adding to nuclear risk, alongside attacks on nuclear facilities and the threat of nuclear use in active conflicts.
source_name: United Nations, close of the 2026 NPT Review Conference

text: Most of the people at risk would be far from the fighting. In the US–Russia scenario, more people would die of famine in India and Pakistan alone than in the countries at war, according to study co-author Alan Robock.
source_name: Live Science, reporting Xia et al., Nature Food, 2022

text: The world warhead total peaks at about 70,300.
source_name: Federation of American Scientists, Status of World Nuclear Forces

source_name: Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, 2026 statement

source_name: UN Secretary-General statement

source_name: United Nations press release

source_name: ICAN

text: Global average surface temperature from January to September 2026 was about 1.47 °C above the pre-industrial average. The past 12 years are the 12 warmest on record.
source_name: World Meteorological Organization, State of the Climate Update for COP31, 2026

text: With the policies governments have in place today, the world is on track for about 2.7 °C of warming by 2100. If every 2030 and 2035 target were met, it would still be 2.6 °C. The Paris Agreement goal is 1.5 °C.
source_name: Climate Action Tracker, Global Update, November 2026

text: Between 2 °C and 3 °C of warming, the West Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets could melt almost completely and irreversibly over many thousands of years, raising sea level by several metres.
source_name: IPCC Sixth Assessment Synthesis Report, 2023 (World Resources Institute summary)

text: Amazon rainforest dieback could happen at about 1.5 °C of warming, and the main Atlantic ocean current system (AMOC) is at risk of collapse below 2 °C. Warm-water coral reefs are already passing their tipping point.
source_name: Global Tipping Points Report 2025 (Zoological Society of London summary)

text: Philosopher Toby Ord puts the chance that climate change causes an existential catastrophe this century at about 1 in 1,000. He says estimates like this could easily be 3 times higher or lower.
source_name: Toby Ord, The Precipice, 2020 (Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews)

text: For comparison, Ord puts the combined chance of an existential catastrophe this century from all causes at about 1 in 6. Climate change is one of several contributors.
source_name: Toby Ord, The Precipice, 2020 (Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews)

text: A 2025 report by 160 scientists warns that as warming exceeds 1.5 °C, multiple tipping points pose catastrophic risks to billions of people.
source_name: Global Tipping Points Report 2025 (Mail & Guardian)

text: UNEP's 'lowest possible' scenario limits peak warming to 1.7–1.8 °C around mid-century and returns to 1.5 °C or below by 2100. It needs global emissions to fall 18% by 2030 and 45% by 2035 from 2025 levels.
source_name: UNEP, Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return

text: Limiting warming to 1.5 °C instead of 2 °C would mean about 420 million fewer people frequently exposed to extreme heatwaves and about 65 million fewer exposed to exceptional heatwaves, assuming people's vulnerability stays the same.
source_name: IPCC, Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5 °C

text: How sensitive the climate is to greenhouse gases is still being revised. The Climate Action Tracker says new evidence suggests the system may be more sensitive than previously thought.
source_name: Climate Action Tracker, Global Update, November 2025

text: Scientists are divided on whether and when the Atlantic ocean current system (AMOC) would collapse. Some studies find a tipping point sometime between 2025 and 2095. Other research finds a collapse unlikely before the end of the century.
source_name: Scientific American, on AMOC stability

text: Climate change has already slowed growth in farm productivity in mid and low latitudes. Droughts, floods and marine heatwaves cut food availability and raise prices, threatening the food security of millions. This topic feeds directly into food security.
source_name: IPCC Sixth Assessment, Working Group II, Chapter 5: Food, Fibre and Other Ecosystem Products

text: Warm-water coral reefs, which nearly a billion people and a quarter of all marine life depend on, are passing their tipping point. This topic feeds directly into nature and biodiversity.
source_name: Global Tipping Points Report 2025 (University of the Witwatersrand release)

text: About 3.3 to 3.6 billion people live in contexts that are highly vulnerable to climate change, according to the IPCC. Those least able to cope are hit hardest.
source_name: IPCC Sixth Assessment, Working Group II, 2022 (Carbon Brief summary)

text: The Climate Action Tracker's assessment of existing policies showed about 3.6 °C of warming by 2100. Its 2026 assessment says 2.7 °C.
source_name: Climate Action Tracker briefing, November 2025

label: 13 Oct 2025
text: The Global Tipping Points Report finds warm-water coral reefs are passing their tipping point, the first Earth system tipping point reached.
source_name: National Oceanography Centre, Global Tipping Points Report 2025

label: 21 Oct 2026
text: UNEP's Emissions Gap Report finds current pledges would cut emissions by only 11–15% by 2035, far short of the 45% needed to return warming to 1.5 °C by 2100.
source_name: Anadolu Agency, reporting UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2026

label: 12 Nov 2026
text: The Climate Action Tracker reports that collective climate action has stalled for a fifth year, with today's policies pointing to 2.7 °C by 2100, up slightly from 2.6 °C last year.
source_name: Climate Action Tracker, Global Update, November 2026

text: COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, is scheduled to close. It opened on 9 November.
source_name: UNFCCC, The Road to Antalya

source_name: Earth Negotiations Bulletin, COP31 daily report, 12 November 2026

text: Monitored wildlife populations fell by an average of 73% between 1970 and 2022. Half of the populations tracked are stable or increasing, but the overall trend is down.
source_name: WWF and Zoological Society of London, Living Planet Report 2026

text: About 1 million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction, many within decades. Around 75% of land and 66% of the ocean have been significantly altered by people.
source_name: IPBES Global Assessment, 2019 (Scientific American summary)

text: Seven of nine planetary boundaries have been breached, including the one for biosphere integrity, and all seven show worsening trends.
source_name: Stockholm Resilience Centre, Planetary Health Check 2025

text: Warm-water coral reefs, which nearly a billion people and a quarter of all marine life depend on, are passing their tipping point.
source_name: Global Tipping Points Report 2025 (University of the Witwatersrand release)

text: The chair of IPBES says the health of the ecosystems that people and all other species depend on is getting worse faster than ever before.
source_name: Sir Robert Watson, IPBES chair (UN Environment Programme release, 2019)

text: Wildlife can rebound when action is taken. WWF points to recoveries of tigers, elephants, turtles and tuna, and half the tracked populations are stable or increasing.
source_name: WWF, Living Planet Report 2026 press release

text: Governments could approach the 30% land target by delivering existing commitments. More than 50 countries and territories already report at least 30% of their land protected or conserved.
source_name: Campaign for Nature, 30x30 Global Assessment 2026

text: Whether protected area coverage measures real protection is disputed. About 20% of land and 10% of the ocean is designated, but one report finds only 3.5% of the ocean is effectively protected, and critics say area coverage does not show how well nature is conserved.
source_name: Campaign for Nature, Ocean Protection Gap Report 2026, and Eco-Business

text: The 73% figure is an average of population trends, not a headcount of animals lost, and it is especially sensitive to changes in already small populations.
source_name: Daily Sabah, reporting the Living Planet Report 2026 (ZSL)

text: Agriculture is one of the biggest threats to ecosystems, and food production depends on healthy ecosystems. This topic feeds directly into food security.
source_name: IPBES Global Assessment, 2019 (Scientific American summary)

text: Climate change is one of the five direct drivers of species decline, so this topic feeds directly into and from climate.
source_name: National Geographic, reporting the IPBES Global Assessment

text: Declines differ by region. Monitored populations in Latin America and the Caribbean fell by about 95% on average, against 28% in North America and 23% in Europe and Central Asia.
source_name: WWF, Living Planet Report 2026 (press release and ZSL via Express & Star)

text: Freshwater populations fell the most, by 85% on average. Terrestrial populations fell 69% and marine populations 59%.
source_name: SDG Knowledge Hub (IISD), Living Planet Report 2026

text: IPBES publishes its Global Assessment, finding about 1 million species threatened with extinction.
source_name: United Nations, IPBES Global Assessment press release

source_name: Convention on Biological Diversity, final text

label: 25 Sep 2025

source_name: Stockholm University, Planetary Health Check 2025

source_name: WWF and Zoological Society of London, Living Planet Report 2026

source_name: Convention on Biological Diversity, State of Biodiversity Action, press release

text: Deadline for the Global Biodiversity Framework's 2030 targets, including protecting 30% of land and sea and restoring 30% of degraded ecosystems.
source_name: Convention on Biological Diversity, 2030 targets

text: The 2026 global hunger score of 18.1 is higher than the 2018 score, which interrupts the decline seen since 2000.
source_name: Global Hunger Index 2026, results

text: About 645 million people faced hunger in 2025, 7.8% of the world, the third yearly fall. This is 43 million fewer people than in 2022.
source_name: PAHO, reporting the UN State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026

text: Famine was confirmed in parts of the Gaza Strip and Sudan in 2025, the first time it was confirmed in two places. 1.4 million people were in the worst food-crisis category, more than nine times the 2016 number.
source_name: Al Jazeera, reporting the Global Report on Food Crises 2026

text: 57 countries will not reach low hunger by 2030 on the current trajectory.
source_name: Global Hunger Index 2026, key numbers (Ayuda en Acción edition)

text: In the food-crisis countries the report covers, 35.5 million children were acutely malnourished in 2025, including nearly 10 million with severe acute malnutrition.
source_name: Down To Earth, reporting the Global Report on Food Crises 2026

text: The rise in hunger in Africa is beginning to level off. The share of its population facing hunger fell from 20.3% in 2024 to 20.0% in 2025.
source_name: PAHO, reporting the UN State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026

text: 31 countries have cut their hunger scores by at least 10% since 2018.
source_name: The Wire, reporting the 2026 Global Hunger Index

text: The two main measures point in different directions. The UN figure tracks undernourishment alone and compares 2025 with 2022. The index adds three child-health measures and compares with 2018, so it can rise while the headcount falls.
source_name: Reset Media, on the Global Hunger Index 2026

text: The index says its scores and rankings cannot be accurately compared with those from earlier reports.
source_name: Global Hunger Index 2026, results

text: The 2026 index finds that not having enough food can deepen vulnerability, increase competition over scarce resources and contribute to instability.
source_name: Global Hunger Index 2026

text: The Russia-Ukraine war has disrupted food and fertiliser markets and raised food prices well beyond the conflict zone.
source_name: Global Hunger Index 2026

text: Africa is home to about 309 million hungry people, against 292 million in Asia.
source_name: UNICEF, State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 (press release)

text: 56.6% of Africa's population was moderately or severely food insecure in 2025, against 20.3% in Asia, 22.9% in Latin America and the Caribbean, and 8.7% in Northern America and Europe.
source_name: IISD SDG Knowledge Hub, on the UN State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026

source_name: FAO and partners, Global Report on Food Crises 2026 (joint news release)

label: 21 Jul 2026
text: The UN reports global hunger fell for a third year, to about 645 million people in 2025.
source_name: FAO, State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 (press release)

label: 14 Oct 2026
text: The 2026 Global Hunger Index finds the global score has risen to 18.1, worse than in 2018. Hunger is alarming in 8 countries and serious in 36.
source_name: Ayuda en Acción, Global Hunger Index 2026 summary

text: Deadline for the UN goal of zero hunger. The 2026 UN report says progress is not enough to reach the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030.
source_name: UNICEF, State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 (press release)

text: Immunization averts an estimated 4.4 million deaths a year.
source_name: UNICEF Data, Vaccination and immunization statistics

text: In 2025, 90% of infants got at least one DTP dose and 85% completed the three-dose series. Both are 1 point below 2019.
source_name: UNICEF and WHO, 2025 immunization coverage estimates (press release, 15 Jul 2026)

text: In 2024, 59 countries reported large or disruptive measles outbreaks, nearly triple the number in 2021.
source_name: WHO, measles deaths down 88% since 2000 (28 Nov 2025)

text: WHO said the impact of aid cuts is not yet fully visible in the 2025 data, and that its concern is for programmes in 2026 and beyond.
source_name: AFP via The Edge Malaysia (21 Jul 2026)

text: Vaccines have saved more than 150 million lives over the past five decades, according to WHO.
source_name: WHO, UNICEF and Gavi, World Immunization Week release (24 Apr 2025)

text: The number of zero-dose children fell by nearly 750,000 in 2025, to about 13.5 million.
source_name: UNICEF and WHO, 2025 immunization coverage estimates (press release, 15 Jul 2026)

text: Lower-income countries immunised a record 73 million children with Gavi-supported vaccines in 2025.
source_name: Gavi, 2025 coverage estimates release (15 Jul 2026)

text: Countries' own reported coverage and the WHO/UNICEF estimates can differ widely. For 2025 the estimate was lower than reported third-dose DTP coverage in 44 countries, 23 of them by more than 10 points.
source_name: WHO and UNICEF, WUENIC 2025 technical notes

text: Afghanistan officially reported 83% third-dose DTP coverage for 2025; the WHO/UNICEF estimate is 61%.
source_name: WHO Immunization Data portal, DTP coverage

text: WHO, UNICEF and Gavi said reduced donor funding is disrupting vaccination campaigns and access to supplies, and that disease surveillance is affected in more than half of the countries surveyed.
source_name: WHO, UNICEF and Gavi, World Immunization Week release (24 Apr 2025)

text: UNICEF's head of immunization said the cuts have hit governments' ability to pay their share of the cost of Gavi vaccines.
source_name: TechNet-21, Big Catch-Up announcement (24 Apr 2026)

text: More than half of zero-dose children live in fragile or conflict-affected settings, which hold about a third of the world's children.
source_name: UNICEF and WHO, 2025 immunization coverage estimates (press release, 15 Jul 2026)

text: More than half of zero-dose children live in nine countries: Afghanistan, Angola, DR Congo, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Nigeria, Pakistan and Yemen.
source_name: UNICEF USA, modest gains in global child immunization (Jul 2026)

source_name: techUK, on the International AI Safety Report 2026
